''''Stone rods''' (せきぼう, sekibō) are a type of polished {{ill|Stone tool|en|Stone tool|qid=Q479257|lt=Stone tool}} from the [[Jōmon period]] in Japan. They are believed to represent [[phalluses]] and are associated with [[:en:Rituals|Rituals]] and [[shamanistic practices]].Yamada 2019: 204

The largest known stone rod is the {{ill|Great Sekibō of Kitazawa|ja|北沢大石棒|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kitazawa Great Stone Rod|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q18457535}} in {{ill|Sakuho, Nagano|en|Sakuho, Nagano|qid=Q1203700|lt=Sakuho, Nagano}}, measuring 223 cm in length and 25 cm in diameter.

== Overview ==
In a broad sense, "stone rods" encompass various rod-shaped stone artifacts, including [[stone swords]] and [[stone daggers]]. In a narrower sense, they often refer specifically to large stone rods.Tori 1924 These artifacts have been found throughout Japan, from [[Kyushu]] to [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]].

Phallic stone artifacts date back to the {{ill|Upper Paleolithic|en|Upper Paleolithic|qid=Q479505|lt=Upper Paleolithic}} period, such as the one found at the {{ill|Masukata Site|ja|升形遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Masukata Site|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Ōami-Shirasato, Chiba|ja|大羽白里市|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōami-Shirasato, Chiba|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, dated to approximately 24,000 years ago.Harunari 1996 The specific type known as "large stone rods" emerged during the Middle Jōmon period in the {{ill|Chūbu region|en|Chūbu region|qid=Q134638|lt=Chūbu region}} and later spread eastward to areas such as the [[:en:Kinki region|Kinki region]].Yamamoto 1979Okada 1960

Sites where stone rods were manufactured have been identified in eastern Japan, such as the {{ill|Shioya Kanesayama Shrine Site|ja|塩屋金清神社遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shioya Kanesayama Shrine Site|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and the {{ill|Shima Site|ja|島遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shima Site|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Gifu Prefecture|en|Gifu Prefecture|qid=Q131277|lt=Gifu Prefecture}},Hayakawa & Hayashi 2000Miyoshi & Nagata 2012 as well as in western Japan, such as the {{ill|Mikuraoka Site|ja|見蔵岡遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mikuraoka Site|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|qid=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture}} and the {{ill|Kamizato Site|ja|上里遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamizato Site|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|qid=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture}}.Matsui, Oshita & Tamura 1997Takahashi & Kondo 2011 These findings suggest that the use of stone rods as ritual objects was adopted as a cultural practice across different regions.Oshita 2001

Some stone rods have been found near the [[:en:hearths|hearths]] of dwellings, often showing signs of heat damage or discoloration. This indicates their use in fire-related [[:en:Rituals|Rituals]]. Ritual practices involving stone rods are thought to symbolically represent the phases of male genital arousal, sexual activity, and post-ejaculatory flaccidity through actions such as striking, heating, and breaking the rods. The prevalence of broken stone rods in archaeological sites has led some researchers to attribute symbolic meanings to this practice, though others remain skeptical.Gotō 1999

Stone rods were also used as burial goods, suggesting multiple [[:en:shamanistic|shamanistic]] or ritualistic purposes.Yamada 2019: 206Taniguchi 2006
